gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the power station's own AC inverter keeps drawing about 10–16 W all night (The Gadgeteer: 10 W on the Elite 200 V2; The Solar Lab: about 16 W on the Elite 100 V2). Against a measured 35 W smoker, that adds 29–46% to an overnight cook. A 12-hour cook then takes about 540–612 Wh from the battery, not the 420 Wh the smoker itself uses. So a 1 kWh station covers about 1.7 overnight cooks and the 2 kWh Elite 200 V2 covers about 3.7.
standout_why: I compared five pages. The Traeger support page (cited) gives grill nameplate watts and nothing about stations. Volt & Valley uses a flat 80% usable figure and an assumed 50 W draw. EcoFlow's blog uses a flat 0.85 and the BLUETTI blog a flat 0.8, and both rest on estimates. Generatorchecker uses a flat 0.70 derate with no idle figure. None of them gives a measured inverter idle draw for any station or separates that fixed hourly cost from the smoker load. At 35 W, a 0.85 derate allows only about 6 W of loss, well below the 10–16 W that reviewers found. Our own current page guesses 10–20 W of inverter draw without a source.
decides: It confirms that 1 kWh is the minimum for one 12-hour night. The Elite 100 V2 runs one night with about 400 Wh left, not the 2+ nights that 0.85-derate arithmetic suggests. It also argues for the Elite 200 V2 when the shopper wants two back-to-back nights without recharging, and it costs less per overnight cook. Our table's '1' for 1 kWh units stands. For the Elite 200 V2, the sourced arithmetic gives about 3.7 rather than 2–3.

findings.label: Measured pellet smoker energy use, 6-hour cook
findings.value: 210 Wh over 6 h (35 W running, about 194 W for several minutes at startup)
findings.source_title: RVelectricity – Pellet Smoker Energy Use (Mike Sokol, Apr 30, 2024)
findings.note: Z Grills smoker (model not named) on a Jackery Explorer 1000. Cook was 3 h at 225°F, then about 3 h at 275°F. 210 Wh ÷ 6 h = 35 W average including startup. The post doesn't give the outside temperature or how it was measured.

findings.label: Smoker energy at the outlet for a 12-hour overnight cook (derived)
findings.note: 35 W × 12 h = 420 Wh. Scaled linearly from one measured 6-hour cook. Cold nights will push it higher.

findings.label: AC idle draw (AC and DC left on)
findings.source_title: The Gadgeteer – BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 review (Greg Cleveland, 2025-01-06, updated 2026-11-02)
findings.note: The page writes '10w/h with AC and DC left on'. I read that as a 10 W rate, which is the same as 10 Wh per hour.

findings.label: Battery Wh per 12-hour smoke (derived)
findings.note: (35 W smoker + 10 W idle) × 12 h = 540 Wh. This treats the 10 W idle as the whole conversion overhead at this light load.

findings.note: $899 ÷ 3.7 cooks = $243. That works out to $899 ÷ 2,000 usable Wh = $0.45 per usable Wh.

findings.label: AC idle draw (inverter on, no load)

findings.label: Battery Wh per 12-hour smoke (derived)
findings.note: (35 W + 16 W idle) × 12 h = 612 Wh. The Solar Lab's 80% efficiency figure gives a lower 525 Wh (420 ÷ 0.80). I used the idle-based figure because the load is light.

findings.label: 12-hour overnight cooks per charge (derived)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 product page (1,024 Wh, 25 lb) + The Solar Lab
findings.note: 1,024 Wh rated ÷ 612 Wh = 1.67. I had no measured usable capacity, so this uses the rated figure and is an upper bound.
